newsitem.title: CANADA: Retailer Eaton's puts sale option on back burner.
newsitem.headline: Retailer Eaton's puts sale option on back burner.

text.p: Canada's venerable retailer T. Eaton Co Ltd, currently under creditor protection, said on Wednesday it has put the option of selling its chain of stores on the back burner as potential stakeholder interest has risen.
"We're quite comfortable (that) the best possible outcome for all the stakeholders is the continuance of the T. Eaton company ... and that's in our plans," chairman George Eaton told reporters.

Eaton said Canada's fifth largest department store chain, privately held by the Eaton family, might have been sold had there been a strong industry player able to put together a better plan than the executives of the beleaguered retailer.
Since the 127-year-old T. Eaton Co filed for bankruptcy protection on February 27, rumors have run rampant that the Canadian retailer would face a buyout by a U.S. firm.
Canadian retailers have lost market share in recent years and some have gone bankrupt due to a weak economy and the 1994 arrival in Canada of Bentonville, Ark.-based discounter Wal-Mart.
Potential investors in Eaton's have been rumored to include J.C. Penney Co Inc, Dillard's Inc and Federated Department Stores Inc.

But the appointment of veteran retailer George Kosich to president of Eaton's from the same position at rival Hudson's Bay Co five weeks ago has sparked increased curiosity amid possible investors, Eaton said.

"We've had interest from potential investors obviously, even prior to George's appointment, but that interest has strengthened and we've had new interest expressed since then," even amid those who had taken a pass the first time around, Eaton said.
Kosich said both Canadian and U.S. financial institutions have been in contact with Eaton's but he ruled out the acquisition of a stake by U.S.-based retailers so far.
Eaton's would need about C$200 million in capital improvements alone over the next five years. It owes about C$210 million to banks and creditors, Eaton said.

He added that his family, one of Canada's wealthiest, might relinquish control or its majority stake during the restructuring process. "Certainly if that worked out where we had majority positions that wouldn't make us unhappy, but we would not hold out for that."
The executives both declined to elaborate on earlier comments by Kosich that Eaton's might be taken public.

Eaton said that U.S. brokerages, such as New York-based Oppenheimer Inc. who have snapped up Eaton's debt from trade creditors, would like to reap cash for their stakes. But they "might like to have some equity," he added.
Eaton and Kosich said that their business plan is almost complete and they expect to refine it in time for the August 15 restructuring deadline.

Eaton's parent, Eaton Group of Companies, has been busy selling real estate and Eaton's, which has said it may sell or close up to 31 of its 85 stores, is changing its pension fund rules to raise money.
Kosich forecast the money-losing retailer would turn a profit this fall.
((Lydia Zajc, Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8100 or lydia.zajc@reuters.com))
